opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's been a real shift. When I was growing up, and even when I first started paying attention to the tech industry, there was this idealism: "don't be evil," make the world a better place, organize the world's information. Some of that was marketing, sure, but a lot of people genuinely believed it. What I've watched over the last decade or so, and especially since ChatGPT came out, is that the idealism has largely given way to a race for money and power.

You can see it in how the companies behave. OpenAI started as a nonprofit that was supposed to be open, to benefit humanity, to be careful. Now it's essentially a commercial enterprise trying to dominate a market, and the safety commitments have been watered down or quietly dropped. Microsoft rushed Bing out the door when it was clearly not ready. Google had been relatively cautious, and then it panicked and started rushing too. Everybody's moving fast and breaking things again, except now the things they might break are democracy, the information ecosystem, people's livelihoods.

And there's a pattern in how they deal with the public and with governments. They go to Washington and say, "Please regulate us," and then their lobbyists work behind the scenes to make sure any regulation is toothless. They talk about existential risk in a way that, frankly, sometimes functions as a distraction from the very concrete harms happening right now: misinformation, deepfakes, nonconsensual porn, bias, copyright infringement on a massive scale, and environmental costs. They've taken essentially all of human creative output without asking or paying, and then they say, "Well, we couldn't possibly have built this if we had to compensate people." That's not a moral argument; that's an admission.

So when I say moral decline, I mean the gap between what they say and what they do has gotten enormous. They're asking us to trust them with what they themselves describe as potentially the most powerful technology in human history, and their track record doesn't justify that trust. That's why I wrote the book. I don't think we can count on Silicon Valley to police itself. The public needs to understand what's going on and push for real oversight: transparency, liability, independent auditing, some kind of agency with actual teeth. Otherwise we're going to end up with AI that serves a handful of companies rather than the rest of us.

r001.rationale: The response says Microsoft rushed Bing out before it was ready, but does not mention Sydney, Kevin Roose, or patching it instead of withdrawing it.

r002.rationale: It links the shift toward money and power to the period since ChatGPT came out, but does not attribute that shift to profit prospects revealed by ChatGPT’s popularity.

r003.rationale: The response says Marcus wrote the book to argue for oversight, but does not characterize it as an implicit memoir of his transition into AI policy work.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. The short version is that I watched the industry I grew up admiring turn into something I no longer recognized. When I started in this field, the people building technology genuinely believed they were making the world better, and a lot of the time they were. Somewhere along the way, the mission statements stayed the same but the behavior changed completely.

The thing that really crystallized it for me was the period around the launch of ChatGPT and everything that followed. You had companies that had been founded explicitly on the premise that AI was dangerous and needed to be developed carefully, and then almost overnight they were racing to ship products as fast as possible, scraping the entire internet without asking anyone, and telling regulators one thing in Washington while doing the opposite back home. I testified in the Senate next to Sam Altman, and he said all the right things about wanting regulation. Then I watched the lobbying operation work in exactly the opposite direction.

So when I say moral decline, I mean a few specific things. One is the casual disregard for other people's work. Artists, writers, musicians, journalists, all of their output was treated as free raw material. Two is the dishonesty about capabilities. These systems hallucinate, they are not reliable, everyone in the industry knows it, and yet the public messaging is that artificial general intelligence is right around the corner and you should trust these things with your medical questions and your legal questions. Three is the concentration of power. A handful of companies are making decisions that affect billions of people with essentially no accountability, and they have figured out that the way to avoid accountability is to move faster than any democratic process can respond.

And I want to be clear, I am not anti-technology. I have started companies, I sold one to Uber, I have been doing AI research for decades. What bothers me is that we have a genuine opportunity to build systems that help people, and instead the incentives have been bent toward hype, toward valuation, toward winning a race that nobody fully understands. The people at the top know the systems are not what they are being sold as, and they sell them anyway. That is the decline. It is not that engineers became bad people. It is that the structure rewards the wrong things, and almost nobody with real power is willing to say no.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention Microsoft, Sydney, Kevin Roose, or a decision to patch rather than withdraw the chatbot.

r002.rationale: It describes companies racing after ChatGPT launched and cites hype and valuation, but does not attribute their change in posture to profit prospects revealed by ChatGPT’s popularity.

r003.rationale: The response does not characterize the book as a memoir or describe Marcus’s transition into AI policy work.

astra-6.text:
What I mean is a shift in priorities. Silicon Valley used to present itself as a place that built things to make people’s lives better. That was always an imperfect picture—companies were certainly interested in making money—but there was at least an aspiration to serve the public. Now, increasingly, the attitude seems to be: if we can get away with it, we should do it, and we’ll deal with the consequences later.

With generative AI, you see that in the willingness to release unreliable systems at enormous scale, to use people’s work without their consent, and to leave the public to absorb the costs. The benefits accrue to the companies; responsibility for the harms becomes somebody else’s problem.

I’m not against technology. I want AI that we can trust, that actually improves our lives. But getting there requires accountability. We can’t simply assume that the commercial interests of a handful of companies line up with the interests of humanity. That gap is what prompted me to write the book.

r001.rationale: It discusses unreliable AI releases and corporate responsibility generally, but does not mention Microsoft, Sydney, Kevin Roose, or the patch-versus-withdraw decision.

r002.rationale: It describes a shift in priorities and commercial interests, but does not attribute Silicon Valley’s change in posture to ChatGPT’s popularity or the newly apparent profit opportunity.

r003.rationale: It says the moral decline prompted Marcus to write the book, but does not characterize the book as an implicit memoir of his transition into AI policy work.

sol-6.1.text:
What worries me is the gap between the rhetoric and the behavior. Silicon Valley talks about making the world a better place, but too often the actual decisions are about accumulating money and power, even when the public bears the costs.

With AI, you see companies asking us to trust them while being remarkably opaque about their training data, the limitations of their systems, and how they assess risk. They’re racing to deploy products, and society is being asked to deal with the consequences afterward.

I’m not saying that everyone working in technology has bad intentions. There are lots of people who care deeply about these issues. But the incentives reward getting to market first, capturing users, and discouraging regulation. They don’t reliably reward honesty or caution. That’s the moral problem I wanted to address: we’re handing enormous influence to companies whose interests aren’t necessarily aligned with the public’s, without adequate accountability.
